claim: Rats exhibit 'empathy' making them a model to understand the neural underpinnings of such behavior.
source: Rats exhibit 'empathy' making them a model to understand the neural underpinnings of such behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and the authors' own experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Behavior and dopamine (DA) release reflects subjective rather than objective evaluation of appetitive and aversive events that occur to another.
source: We show data consistent with these findings, but also that behavior and dopamine (DA) release reflects subjective rather than objective evaluation of appetitive and aversive events that occur to another.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both paradigms showing differential DA responses to self vs. other outcomes.

claim: DA suppression was reduced during cues that predicted shock in the presence of the conspecific.
source: DA suppression was reduced during cues that predicted shock in the presence of the conspecific
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data comparing alone vs. together conditions during shock-self trials.

claim: DA release observed on self-avoidance trials was present when the conspecific was spared.
source: DA release observed on self-avoidance trials was present when the conspecific was spared.
evidence: This is supported by DA measurements during the instrumental task on shock-other no-press trials.

claim: DA increased when the conspecific was shocked instead of the recording rat.
source: However, DA also increased when the conspecific was shocked instead of the recording rat
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data during shock-other trials in the Pavlovian paradigm.

claim: DA release during conspecific avoidance trials was lower than when the rat avoided shock for itself.
source: DA release during conspecific avoidance trials was lower than when the rat avoided shock for itself.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between shock-self no-press and shock-other no-press trials.

claim: The ability to appropriately adjust behavior in a social context is impacted in several psychiatric disorders.
source: The ability to appropriately adjust behavior in a social context is performed daily and is impacted in several psychiatric disorders (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Blair, 2003; Cook and Black, 2012; Gaigg, 2012; Hamilton, 2013; Matthys et al., 2013; Neuhaus et al., 2010; Rizzolatti and Fabbri-Destro, 2008; Scott-Van Zeeland et al., 2010; Taylor and DeQuinzio, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature on psychiatric disorders.

claim: Rodent models can be used to study social behavior at the single-unit and neurotransmitter level.
source: A growing number of high-profile reports have demonstrated that rodent models can be used to perform such experiments (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Church, 1959; Guzmán et al., 2009; Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2018; Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2018; Hernandez-Lallement et al., 2017; Jeon et al., 2010; Jones et al., 2014; Kashtelyan et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2010; Langford et al., 2006; Masserman et al., 1964; Meyza et al., 2017; Mogil, 2015; Panksepp, 2011; Panksepp and Lahvis, 2011; Sato et al., 2015; Schaich Borg et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous rodent social behavior studies.

claim: Rats freeze when they see others freeze in response to threat.
source: For example, rats have been described as 'empathetic' and 'prosocial' because they freeze when they see others freeze in response to threat and will rescue conspecifics from distress when given the opportunity (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Meyza et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating this behavior.

claim: Rats will rescue conspecifics from distress when given the opportunity.
source: For example, rats have been described as 'empathetic' and 'prosocial' because they freeze when they see others freeze in response to threat and will rescue conspecifics from distress when given the opportunity (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Meyza et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating rescue behavior.

claim: Prosocial behaviors are particularly strong when rats are cage mates.
source: These prosocial behaviors are particularly strong when rats are cage mates and in situations in which there are no explicit negative consequences to the rat performing the prosocial act.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies in the field.

claim: Rats can be more interested in their own physical state (subjective value) as opposed to another's (objective value).
source: Here, we show that rats can be more interested in their own physical state (subjective value) as opposed to another's (objective value), which we will refer to as 'self-interested'.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and DA data from both experimental paradigms.

claim: Subsecond dopamine (DA) release in nucleus accumbens core (NAc) accompanies regard for one's own interest, reflecting the subjective value placed on appetitive and aversive events.
source: Further, we demonstrate that subsecond dopamine (DA) release in nucleus accumbens core (NAc) accompanies this regard for one's own interest, reflecting the subjective value placed on appetitive and aversive events as opposed to the objective value of the event itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltammetry data showing differential DA responses to self vs. other outcomes.

claim: The DA system is the only neurotransmitter system that genuinely signals all aspects of reward prediction error encoding.
source: The DA system is unique in that it is the only neurotransmitter system that genuinely signals all aspects of reward prediction error encoding (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Day et al., 2007; Gan et al., 2010; Hart et al., 2015; Hart et al., 2015; Roesch et al., 2010; Schultz, 2010; Schultz et al., 2015; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous literature on dopamine signaling.

claim: DA neurons in the VTA and DA release into the NAc increases in response to events that are better than expected.
source: By using a variety of technical approaches across species, studies have shown that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and subsequent DA release into the NAc increases and decreases in response to events that are better or worse than expected, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations.

claim: DA neurons in the VTA and DA release into the NAc decreases in response to events that are worse than expected.
source: By using a variety of technical approaches across species, studies have shown that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and subsequent DA release into the NAc increases and decreases in response to events that are better or worse than expected, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations.

claim: Cues that predict reward or the uncertain delivery of reward increase DA release.
source: In the appetitive domain, cues that predict reward or the uncertain delivery of reward increase DA release, and cues that predict less favorable reward and omission of expected reward decrease DA release.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous dopamine research.

claim: Cues that predict less favorable reward and omission of expected reward decrease DA release.
source: In the appetitive domain, cues that predict reward or the uncertain delivery of reward increase DA release, and cues that predict less favorable reward and omission of expected reward decrease DA release.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous dopamine research.

claim: Cues predictive of unavoidable aversive events robustly reduce DA release.
source: In aversive contexts, cues predictive of unavoidable aversive events (e.g., quinine, air puff, shock) or delivery of those aversive outcomes themselves robustly reduce DA release, whereas unexpected omission of aversive events or the cues that predict avoidable shock reliably elicit phasic DA release (McCutcheon et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Wenzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on aversive DA signaling.

claim: Delivery of aversive outcomes robustly reduces DA release.
source: In aversive contexts, cues predictive of unavoidable aversive events (e.g., quinine, air puff, shock) or delivery of those aversive outcomes themselves robustly reduce DA release, whereas unexpected omission of aversive events or the cues that predict avoidable shock reliably elicit phasic DA release (McCutcheon et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Wenzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on aversive DA signaling.

claim: Unexpected omission of aversive events reliably elicits phasic DA release.
source: In aversive contexts, cues predictive of unavoidable aversive events (e.g., quinine, air puff, shock) or delivery of those aversive outcomes themselves robustly reduce DA release, whereas unexpected omission of aversive events or the cues that predict avoidable shock reliably elicit phasic DA release (McCutcheon et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Wenzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on aversive DA signaling.

claim: Cues that predict avoidable shock reliably elicit phasic DA release.
source: In aversive contexts, cues predictive of unavoidable aversive events (e.g., quinine, air puff, shock) or delivery of those aversive outcomes themselves robustly reduce DA release, whereas unexpected omission of aversive events or the cues that predict avoidable shock reliably elicit phasic DA release (McCutcheon et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Wenzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on aversive DA signaling.

claim: DA release was recorded from eight rats during performance of the Pavlovian Social Distress Paradigm.
source: DA release was recorded from eight rats during performance of the Pavlovian Social Distress Paradigm, during which pairs of rats were placed side by side in a modified shuttle box, separated by a modified guillotine door that allowed rats to see, smell, and hear each other (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methods used.

claim: Rats were placed side by side in a modified shuttle box, separated by a modified guillotine door that allowed rats to see, smell, and hear each other.
source: DA release was recorded from eight rats during performance of the Pavlovian Social Distress Paradigm, during which pairs of rats were placed side by side in a modified shuttle box, separated by a modified guillotine door that allowed rats to see, smell, and hear each other (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Recording rats correctly internalized auditory and directional light cues.
source: Because the task was Pavlovian (i.e., no instrumental component) we used bream breaks in the food cup and video scoring to determine if recording rats understood the different trial-types.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing differential responses to different cue types.

claim: Percent beam breaks increased on reward-self trials relative to neutral trials prior to outcome delivery.
source: Prior to outcome delivery, percent beam breaks respectively increased and decreased on reward-self (blue) and shock-self (red) trials relative to neutral (green) trials (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Percent beam breaks decreased on shock-self trials relative to neutral trials prior to outcome delivery.
source: Prior to outcome delivery, percent beam breaks respectively increased and decreased on reward-self (blue) and shock-self (red) trials relative to neutral (green) trials (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There was a significant increase in beam breaks in the food cup for reward-self compared to reward-other trials after presentation of the directional light cue.
source: After the presentation of the directional light cue (i.e., the cue that informed the rat which animal would receive the outcome), there was a significant increase in beam breaks in the food cup for reward-self compared to reward-other trials (Figure 2A versus B; blue; Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: During shock trials, there was a general suppression of beam breaks across both 'self' and 'other' trial-types, with little difference between them.
source: During shock trials, there was a general suppression across both 'self' (Figure 2A; red) and 'other' trial-types (Figure 2B; red), with little difference between them.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rats visited the food cup significantly more often on reward-other trials when they were alone.
source: For reward-self trials this distribution was not significantly shifted (Figure 2K; Wilcoxon; u = 0.20; p = 0.30), however the distribution of indices were shifted in the positive direction for reward-other trials (Figure 2N; Wilcoxon; u = 0.38; p < 0.05). Thus, rats visited the food cup significantly more often on reward-other trials when they were alone.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: The distribution of 'alone minus together' indices for shock-self trials were shifted in the negative direction, almost reaching significance.
source: For shock-self, the distribution of 'alone minus together' indices were shifted in the negative direction, almost reaching significance (Figure 2M; Wilcoxon; u = −0.09; p = 0.057), possibly reflecting reduced fear when together with the other rat.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Rats froze significantly more often on shock-self trials compared to other trial types during the directional light epoch, both when together and alone.
source: Freezing was defined as the absence of movement except for respiration. As for the analysis of beam breaks into the food cup, it was clear that rats understood the meaning of the cues; rats froze significantly more often on shock-self trials compared to other trial types during the directional light epoch, both when together and alone (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by video scoring data and statistical analysis.

claim: Rats froze significantly more on alone-shock-self trials compared to together-shock-other trials.
source: Also, consistent with the suppression observed on alone-shock-self trials, rats froze significantly more on alone-shock-self trials compared to together-shock-other trials (Figure 3A; red; left versus right panels), suggesting less fear during cues that predicted self-shock when rats were together.
evidence: This is supported by video scoring data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Significant increases in freezing were not observed on shock trials compared to neutral trials during directional cue and outcome epochs for 'other' trials.
source: These effects on freezing were absent during 'other' trials; significant increases in freezing were not observed on shock trials compared to neutral trials during directional cue and outcome epochs (Figure 3C and D; Wilcoxons; p's > 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of video scoring data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Rats did not overly exhibit freezing behavior during observation of another rat freezing during cues that predict shock or observation of shock itself.
source: Thus, under our experimental conditions, rats did not overly exhibit freezing behavior during observation of another rat freezing during cues that predict shock or observation of shock itself, at least when comparing freezing during together-shock-other trials to alone-shock-other and neutral-other trials.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of freezing data across trial types.

claim: Rats freeze similarly to self-shock and conspecific-shock.
source: However, freezing between together-shock-self and together-shock-other comparisons (i.e., red bar in Figure 3A with the open red bar in Figure 3C) showed that rats freeze similarly to self-shock and conspecific-shock, consistent with the existing literature.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of freezing data and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Rats froze more on shock trials when alone compared to when they were together.
source: To further quantify this effect we ran a 3-factor ANOVA (together vs alone; self vs other; trial-type (i.e., reward, neutral, shock) on freezing during the directional cue. Significant main effects of together/alone (F(1,396) = 4.44; p < 0.05) and trial-type (F(2,396) = 16.48; p < 0.05), as well as a significant interaction between self/other and trial-type (F(2,396) = 3.3; p < 0.05) were observed. Thus, rats froze more on shock trials when alone compared to when they were together.
evidence: This is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of freezing data.

claim: Freezing was significantly stronger on self-shock trials when alone compared to when rats were together.
source: Furthermore, post-hoc t tests demonstrate that freezing was significantly stronger on self-shock trials when alone compared to when rats were together (t(33) = 2.54; p < 0.05) and that freezing did not significantly differ on together-self-shock and together-other-shock trials (t(33) = 0.19; p = 0.85).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc t-test analysis of freezing data.

claim: Freezing did not significantly differ on together-self-shock and together-other-shock trials.
source: Furthermore, post-hoc t tests demonstrate that freezing was significantly stronger on self-shock trials when alone compared to when rats were together (t(33) = 2.54; p < 0.05) and that freezing did not significantly differ on together-self-shock and together-other-shock trials (t(33) = 0.19; p = 0.85).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc t-test analysis of freezing data.

claim: Rats approached the conspecific's side of the box most often on together-shock-self trials.
source: Rats approached the conspecific's side of the box most often on together-shock-self trials (Figure 3F; red).
evidence: This is supported by video scoring data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Percent approach was significantly higher on together-shock trials compared to alone-shock-self and together-neutral-self trials for both 'self' and 'other' trial-types.
source: For both 'self' and 'other' trial-types, percent approach was significantly higher on together-shock trials compared to alone-shock-self and together-neutral-self trials (Figure 3F and H; Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of approach behavior shown in Figure 3F and H.

claim: The recording rat approached the conspecific more during together-shock-self relative to together-shock-other trials.
source: Although the recording rat approached the conspecific both during self and other shock trials, this effect was stronger when the threat was to the recording rat (together-shock-self versus together-shock-other; Figure 3F versus Figure 3H; red; Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of approach behavior shown in Figure 3F and H.

claim: Approach was driven by the desire for social contact and shock, but only when the recording rat was threatened.
source: These results suggest that approach was driven by the desire for social contact (i.e., more approach when the conspecific was present than when alone) and shock (i.e., more approach during shock trials than reward and neutral), but only when the recording rat was threatened (i.e., more approach during together-self-shock relative to together-shock-other trials).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of approach behavior across conditions.

claim: When rats were alone, average DA release increased to cues that predicted reward-self trials significantly more than neutral trials.
source: Consistent with this previous work, we found that when rats were alone, average DA release over all sessions (n = 40) increased to cues that predicted reward-self trials (blue) significantly more than neutral trials (green) during presentation of cues and reward (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data shown in Figure 4A and statistical analysis.

claim: DA release was lower during presentation of cues that predicted unavoidable shock when rats were alone.
source: and that DA release was lower during presentation of cues that predicted unavoidable shock (Figure 4A; red (shock) versus green (neutral) when alone (thin) during directional light cue presentations).
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The distributions of reward indices were significantly shifted in the positive direction indicating significantly higher DA release on reward trials relative to neutral trials during alone trials.
source: The distributions of reward and shock indices were significantly shifted in the positive and negative direction indicating significantly higher (Figure 4F; Wilcoxon; µ = 24.6; p < 0.05) and lower (Figure 4G; Wilcoxon; µ = −11.5; p < 0.05) DA release on reward and shock trials relative to neutral trials, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The distributions of shock indices were significantly shifted in the negative direction indicating significantly lower DA release on shock trials relative to neutral trials during alone trials.
source: The distributions of reward and shock indices were significantly shifted in the positive and negative direction indicating significantly higher (Figure 4F; Wilcoxon; µ = 24.6; p < 0.05) and lower (Figure 4G; Wilcoxon; µ = −11.5; p < 0.05) DA release on reward and shock trials relative to neutral trials, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The decline of DA release induced by the presentation of shock-self cues was attenuated in the presence of the conspecific.
source: However, during shock-self trials, we found that the decline of DA release induced by the presentation of shock-self cues was attenuated in the presence of the conspecific (Figure 4A; thick versus thin red lines after outcome cue onset).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between alone and together conditions shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The distribution of 'shock minus neutral' indices calculated on shock-self trials were not significantly shifted when rats were together.
source: Consistent with this observation, the distribution of 'shock minus neutral' indices calculated on shock-self trials were not significantly shifted (Figure 4I; Wilcoxon; µ = −1.4; p = 0.43) as they were during alone-shock-self trials (Figure 4G; Wilcoxon; µ = −11.5; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: After the cue signaled a reward trial, there was an increase in DA release above neutral cues similar to what was observed during reward-self trials.
source: After the cue signaled a reward trial, there was an increase in DA release above neutral cues similar to what was observed during reward-self trials (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data during reward-other trials.

claim: Immediately after illumination of the directional light cue, DA release declined to pre-cue levels for both 'alone' and 'together' trials during reward-other trials.
source: Only after directional cue presentation did rats become aware of who would receive the reward. In line with rats being self-interested, immediately after illumination of the directional light cue, DA release declined to pre-cue levels for both 'alone' and 'together' trials.
evidence: This is supported by DA data during reward-other trials shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DA release was significantly lower when reward was delivered to the conspecific compared to when reward was delivered to the recording rat.
source: As a result, DA release was significantly lower when reward was delivered to the conspecific compared to when reward was delivered to the recording rat (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of DA signals between reward-self and reward-other trials.

claim: There were no significant differences in DA release between alone and together reward-other trials during the outcome epoch.
source: This was true for both 'alone' and 'together' trials and there were no significant differences between them during the outcome epoch (Figure 5B; Wilcoxon; µ = −1.12; p = 0.86), which suggest that DA release during reward-other trials was not modulated by social context.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DA release during reward-other trials was not modulated by social context.
source: This was true for both 'alone' and 'together' trials and there were no significant differences between them during the outcome epoch (Figure 5B; Wilcoxon; µ = −1.12; p = 0.86), which suggest that DA release during reward-other trials was not modulated by social context.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of difference between alone and together conditions.

claim: Prior to shock delivery, DA release was similar during the outcome cue and directional cue epochs on shock-other trials.
source: Although DA release on reward-other trials was not modulated by presence of the conspecific, shock-other trials were. Prior to shock delivery DA release was similar during the outcome cue and directional cue epochs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DA release was not different on shock-other trials compared to together-shock-self trials.
source: In fact, DA release was not different on shock-other trials compared to together-shock-self trials, reminiscent of the observation described above that rats froze at a similar level on together-shock-other compared to together-shock-self trials.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals across trial types.

claim: There was no significant difference between together-self-shock and together-conspecific-shock trials in DA release during the directional cue epoch.
source: Post-hoc t-tests yield a significant difference between alone-shock-self and together-shock-self (t(39) = 3.53; p < 0.05) consistent with the analysis described above, and no significant difference between together-self-shock and together-conspecific-shock trials (t(39) = 1.95; p = 0.06).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc t-test analysis of DA data.

claim: After shock was delivered to the conspecific, DA release actually increased.
source: Although prior to shock delivery, DA release was similar for together-shock-self, together-shock-other and alone-shock-other trials, we found that after shock was delivered to the conspecific, DA release actually increased (Figure 5A; thick red)
evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DA release was significantly higher following shock delivery to the conspecific compared to neutral trials.
source: DA release was significantly higher following shock delivery to the conspecific compared to neutral trials (Figure 5A; thick red versus thick green; Figure 5I; Wilcoxon; µ = 7.4; p < 0.05)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: DA release was significantly higher following shock delivery to the conspecific compared to when shock was delivered to the conspecific's empty side of the cage.
source: and compared to when shock was delivered to the conspecific's empty side of the cage (Figure 5A; thick red versus thin red; Figure 5D; Wilcoxon; µ = −8.6; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Rats took longer and were less likely to lever press on shock-other trials relative to non-shock trials.
source: Over all recording sessions (n = 24), rats took longer (Figure 6F) and were less likely (Figure 1E) to lever press on shock-other trials relative to non-shock trials (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05) consistent with previous reports suggesting thats rat do perform 'prosocial' acts to benefit others in distress (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Meyza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E and F and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Rats refrained from pressing significantly more often and were significantly slower when the auditory cues signaled shock to oneself as opposed to the conspecific.
source: However, behavior was also strongly guided by individual outcomes rather than those of the conspecific. That is, rats refrained from pressing significantly more often and were significantly slower when the auditory cues signaled shock to oneself as opposed to the conspecific (Figure 6E and F; red vs orange; Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Rats approached the conspecific on 24% of footshock trials, but only following the lever press.
source: On footshock trials, rats approached the conspecific on 24% of trials, but only following the lever press (Figure 6G; orange; 23% after lever press; 1% after no lever press; chi-square, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by video scoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Rats occasionally approached the conspecific after the lever press on no-shock trials.
source: Interestingly, rats also occasionally approached the conspecific after the lever press on no-shock trials (Figure 6G; blue; 13% after lever press; 1% after no lever press; chi-square, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by video scoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cues that predict avoidable shock increase DA release to a similar degree as cues that predict reward delivery.
source: Although cues that predict unavoidable footshock suppress DA release (as in the Pavlovian Social Distress Paradigm described above; Figure 4), recent work has shown that cues that predict avoidable shock and avoidance of shock itself, DA release increases to a similar degree as to cues that predict reward delivery (Gentry et al., 2016; Oleson and Cheer, 2013; Oleson et al., 2012; Wenzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the current data.

claim: DA release was observed on both reward and shock-self cues, with no difference between them.
source: Figure 7 illustrates DA release over all recording sessions (n = 24) when rats pressed for reward (blue) and did not press to avoid self-shock (red). DA release was observed on both reward and shock-self cues, with no difference between them.
evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The distribution of differences between DA release on reward press and shock-self no press trials is not significantly shifted.
source: This is quantified in Figure 7C, which plots the difference between DA release on reward press and shock-self no press trials (shock minus reward) for each session. The distribution is not significantly shifted indicating no differences between reward and shock-self trials (Wilcoxon; µ = −1.9; p = 0.95).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A similar pattern of DA release emerged during shock-other no press trials as during non-press shock-self trials, but the magnitude of DA release was significantly lower on shock-other no press trials.
source: Orange lines in Figure 7A represent shock-other trials when the recording rat did not press the lever for reward, thus avoiding shock for the conspecific. Remarkably a similar pattern of DA release emerged as during non-press shock-self trials, with DA release to the cue and during the absence of the shock; however, the magnitude of DA release was significantly lower on shock-other no press trials (orange) compared to when rats avoided self-shock (red) and when the rats pressed the lever on no-shock reward trials when there was no threat of shock (blue).
evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 7A and statistical analysis.

claim: DA release was significantly lower on shock-other trials relative to no-shock trials.
source: This is quantified in Figure 7B and D, which plot the distributions of differences between shock-other and shock-self (shock-self minus shock-other), and between no-shock and shock-other trials (shock-other minus no-shock). Both distributions were significantly shifted (Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05; Figure 7B and D) indicating significantly lower DA release on shock-other trials relative to no-shock trials
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: DA release was significantly higher on shock-self relative to shock-other trials.
source: This is quantified in Figure 7B and D, which plot the distributions of differences between shock-other and shock-self (shock-self minus shock-other), and between no-shock and shock-other trials (shock-other minus no-shock). Both distributions were significantly shifted (Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05; Figure 7B and D) indicating significantly lower DA release on shock-other trials relative to no-shock trials and significantly higher DA release on shock-self relative to shock-other trials.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: Patients with psychopathic traits and autism have difficulties recognizing the mental states of others and appropriately altering behavior in social contexts.
source: Importantly, patients with psychopathic traits and autism have difficulties recognizing the mental states of others and appropriately altering behavior in social contexts (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Blair, 2003; Buckholtz et al., 2010; Cook and Black, 2012; Gaigg, 2012; Hamilton, 2013; Matthys et al., 2013; Neuhaus et al., 2010; Rizzolatti and Fabbri-Destro, 2008; Scott-Van Zeeland et al., 2010; Taylor and DeQuinzio, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous clinical literature.

claim: These disorders are difficult to treat and currently lack effective pharmacological interventions.
source: These disorders are difficult to treat and currently lack effective pharmacological interventions, reflecting the lack of knowledge pertaining to our understanding of the underlying neurobiology of how social cues may alter behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about psychiatric disorders.

claim: Rats will choose mutual reward in a prosocial task.
source: For example, rats will choose mutual reward in a prosocial task, freeze when they see another rat freeze (interpreted as 'empathy') and exhibit 'prosocial' rescue behavior of a conspecific in distress.
evidence: This claim is based on previous literature on rat social behavior.

claim: Rats will rescue a conspecific that is confined in a restrainer, even when faced with a choice between freeing the trapped rat and obtaining food reward.
source: Most notable was a recent set of high profile papers (Science; eLife) demonstrating that rats will rescue a conspecific that is confined in a restrainer, even when faced with a choice between freeing the trapped rat and obtaining food reward (Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific high-profile studies.

claim: Rats only freeze when they have experienced shock themselves.
source: Although many of these studies are intriguing, they have met criticism; effects are often small, rats only freeze when they have experienced shock themselves, and rats do not free trapped conspecifics under all circumstances (Schwartz et al., 2017; Silberberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to critical literature.

claim: Rats do not free trapped conspecifics under all circumstances.
source: Although many of these studies are intriguing, they have met criticism; effects are often small, rats only freeze when they have experienced shock themselves, and rats do not free trapped conspecifics under all circumstances (Schwartz et al., 2017; Silberberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to critical literature.

claim: 'Prosocial' rescue behavior might reflect some sort of reproductive benefit.
source: Further, many of these effects are dependent on rats being cage mates or of the same strain, suggesting that 'prosocial' rescue behavior might reflect some sort of reproductive benefit.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns in the literature.

claim: Cues and outcomes directed to the conspecific did not produce the same pattern of DA results as those directed to the recording rat.
source: Importantly, cues and outcomes directed to the conspecific did not produce the same pattern of results, suggesting that – if DA signals genuinely reflect value of predictive cues – cues that predicted conspecific reward and shock were not considered to be appetitive and aversive, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between self and other trials.

claim: Footshocks directed to the conspecific actually increased DA release.
source: Moreover, footshocks directed to the conspecific actually increased DA release, suggesting that rats may have been using cues from conspecific (e.g., vocalizations, odors, visual, etc.) to determine that the shock had been delivered to the conspecific, signaling the value of personal safety or relief.
evidence: This is supported by DA data during shock-other trials and is an interpretation of the signal.

claim: The recording rat approached the other rat during the outcome, but did not freeze.
source: This interpretation is supported by the freezing and approach behavior at the time of the shock. The rat that we recorded from approached the other rat during the outcome, but did not freeze.
evidence: This is supported by video scoring data during shock-other trials.

claim: The recording rat was engaged with the conspecific possibly to determine what will occur during the trial, but was not overly fearful during that period.
source: This suggests that the recording rat was engaged with the conspecific possibly to determine what will occur during the trial, but was not overly fearful during that period (i.e., the period when DA increases during conspecific shock).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of approach and freezing behavior.

claim: The presence of the other rat altered the subjective value placed on cues that predicted self-shock by reducing fear and the associated suppression of the DA signal during the Pavlovian paradigm.
source: Remarkably, we also found that the presence of the other rat altered the subjective value placed on cues that predicted self-shock by reducing fear and the associated suppression of the DA signal during the Pavlovian paradigm.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA and behavioral data between alone and together conditions.

claim: The recording rat approached the conspecific on shock-self trials, perhaps reflecting 'consolation' seeking behavior similar to what has been described in prairie voles.
source: On these trials the rat approached the conspecific, perhaps reflecting 'consolation' seeking behavior similar to what has been described in prairie voles (Burkett et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on approach behavior and comparison to previous literature.

claim: The lack of suppression of DA release during shock-self trials when together suggests that the recording rat found the shock cue to be subjectively less aversive in the presence of the conspecific.
source: The lack of suppression of DA release during this period suggests that the recording rat found the shock cue to be subjectively less aversive in the presence of the conspecific.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on DA data during together-shock-self trials.

claim: Rats entered the food cup and froze less often on together-shock-self trials.
source: Indeed, rats entered the food cup and froze less often on together-shock-self trials.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing alone and together shock-self trials.

claim: In the instrumental task, rats pressed significantly less and were slower to press on conspecific-shock trials.
source: In the context of the instrumental task rats pressed significantly less and were slower to press on conspecific-shock trials, demonstrating empathetic and prosocial behaviors consistent with previous reports (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Meyza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the instrumental task and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: DA release during decisions to give up reward and spare the conspecific from shock mirrored DA release when the rat avoided shock for itself.
source: Remarkably, DA release during decisions to give up reward and spare the conspecific from shock mirrored DA release when the rat avoided shock for itself, suggesting that DA release during conspecific shock trials reflected the value of saving the conspecific similar to when it signals the value of saving oneself and that the same signal that encourages avoiding shock for oneself is present when avoiding shock for a conspecific.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between shock-self and shock-other avoidance trials.

claim: Lever pressing increased and DA release decreased during conspecific-shock compared to self-shock.
source: However, lever pressing increased and DA release decreased during conspecific-shock compared to self-shock, which indicates that rats were more interested in sparing themselves from harm rather than sparing the conspecific.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of behavioral and DA data between shock-self and shock-other trials.

claim: The DA signal is modulated by the degree of 'empathy' exhibited by rats in the context of this task.
source: This suggests that the DA signal is modulated by the degree of 'empathy' exhibited by rats in the context of this task.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of DA signals across conditions.

claim: Rats do not always demonstrate 'empathetic' and 'prosocial' behavior as described previously or as expected in humans.
source: The behavior described here demonstrates that rats do not always demonstrate 'empathetic' and 'prosocial' behavior as described previously or as expected in humans.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the overall pattern of behavioral results.

claim: Each task structure promotes different levels of 'pro-social' and 'empathetic' behavior along a continuum.
source: Importantly, across studies (ours and others) we don't think that these differences reflect problems with task design (ours or others), but that each task structure promotes different levels of 'pro-social' and 'empathetic' behavior along a continuum, providing insights into social behavior, and how the brain governs behavior and interprets outcomes in social contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the nature of prosocial behavior across different experimental contexts.

claim: DA release is modulated by social context in at least three ways.
source: For the first time, we show that DA release is modulated by social context in at least three ways.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the three specific findings described next.

claim: Reductions in DA release during cues that predict foot shock were weaker in the presence of the conspecific.
source: First, reductions in DA release during cues that predict foot shock were weaker in the presence of the conspecific, likely due to comfort or distraction of being in the presence of another rat as evidenced by seeking social contact prior to and during foot shock delivery when together, but not alone.
evidence: This is supported by DA and behavioral data comparing alone and together shock-self trials.

claim: DA release during shock trials increased when shock was administered to the conspecific.
source: Second, DA release during shock trials increased when shock was administered to the conspecific, demonstrating that DA release was modulated by conspecific cues that indicated that the foot shock had occurred on the other side of the box.
evidence: This is supported by DA data during shock-other trials.

claim: During the instrumental task, cues that predict avoidable foot shock for the conspecific elicited a similar, but weaker DA release compared to cues that predicted avoidable foot shock for oneself.
source: Third, during the instrumental task, cues that predict avoidable foot shock for the conspecific elicited a similar, but weaker DA release compared to cues that predicted avoidable foot shock for oneself.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between shock-self and shock-other avoidance trials.

claim: DA release is modulated by social context in that rats use social cues to optimize predictions about their own self-interest, even at the expense of a conspecific.
source: Overall, we conclude that DA release is modulated by social context in that rats use social cues to optimize predictions about their own self-interest, even at the expense of a conspecific, and that correlates related to avoidance are present, albeit weaker, when consequences are directed to another rat as opposed to oneself.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of all the DA findings in the study.
